section_title: Has God abandoned the exiles, or will He give them a new heart?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 13 Now as I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died. Then I fell facedown and cried out in a loud voice, “Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?” 14 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 15 “Son of man, your brothers—your relatives, your fellow exiles, and the whole house of Israel—are those of whom the people of Jerusalem have said, ‘They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession.’ 16 Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Although I sent them far away among the nations and scattered them among the countries, yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone.’

17 Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you from the countries to which you have been scattered, and I will give back to you the land of Israel.’ 18 When they return to it, they will remove all its detestable things and all its abominations. 19 And I will give them singleness of heart and put a new spirit within them; I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh, 20 so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God. 21 But as for those whose hearts pursue detestable things and abominations, I will bring their conduct down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.”

context_lines: While Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah dies. Ezekiel falls facedown and again asks whether the Lord will bring Israel’s remnant to a complete end. The answer turns his attention to those already scattered.

The people remaining in Jerusalem have treated the exiles as far from the Lord and claimed the land for themselves. God answers that, although He sent the exiles away, He has been a sanctuary for them in the countries where they have gone. Distance from the temple has not placed them beyond His care.

He promises to gather them, return the land and remove its detestable worship. The restoration includes something deeper than returning home: He will give them singleness of heart and a new spirit, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh.

The contrast describes a change from stubborn refusal to a heart responsive to God. Its purpose is lived obedience: they will follow His statutes and belong to Him as His people. Those whose hearts continue to pursue the detestable things remain accountable for their conduct.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/11.htm) connects the promised return and renewed unity with the exiles’ return under Cyrus and the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s worship. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/11.htm) emphasizes the inward change God gives, applying the heart of flesh to people made responsive to Him through Christ.

[John Walvoord’s account of Israel’s restoration](https://walvoord.com/article/26) places national restoration and spiritual renewal at Christ’s return. It represents a future fulfillment reading, rather than treating return from Babylon as the completion of Israel’s promised restoration.

The readings differ over the extent and timing of fulfillment. The passage itself joins return, the removal of idols, inward renewal and obedience. Its hope rests on what God promises to give, while its final warning still addresses those who cling to wrongdoing.
god_plan_lines: The heart-and-Spirit promise is developed further in [Ezekiel 36:22–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ezekiel/36.htm), where God promises cleansing and the gift of His Spirit so His people will walk in His ways.

[Romans 8:1–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/8.htm) explains how God acts through His Son and His indwelling Spirit to free those in Christ from sin and death. Paul is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 11, but he develops the larger theme of life and obedience made possible by God’s work within His people.

The promise of God’s presence also reaches beyond access to a particular building. [Ephesians 2:17–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/2.htm) describes people once far away gaining access to the Father through Christ and being built together into a dwelling for God by His Spirit. These connections show why restoration involves both belonging to God and a changed life.
